attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. He cites MIT, McKinsey and Bain as sources but makes the assertion himself and endorses it.

semantics.note: Keeps the output-versus-returns contrast and the 'many companies' qualifier. The GDP clause is left out and scoped out explicitly, which is acceptable. The claim is unhedged and about the present, so it is an observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: 'many' means a substantial group, not a majority, and 'much RoI' means meaningful realised financial benefit. The one-year window ending at publication is the evaluator's choice but reasonable. The contradiction condition correctly says that some companies succeeding does not defeat 'many'.

evidence.note: PwC CEO survey, collected Sep–Nov 2025, inside the window. 56% of CEOs report no significant financial benefit from AI so far, which is a substantial group.
Deloitte survey of organisations with working AI, collected Aug–Sep 2025, inside the window. Only 10–15% report significant measurable ROI, so many adopters lack meaningful returns.
Bloomberg report on a Bain survey completed April 2026. AI cost savings often fell short of expectations, but savings are not ROI and the original report is unavailable, so this is context only.

Dun & Bradstreet survey, 2026. 60% report at least some measurable ROI and 24% broad or strong returns. That still leaves about 40% with none and most with only partial returns, so it does not show limited returns are exceptional.

reviews.rationale: Two original surveys collected inside the window show a substantial share of companies without meaningful realised financial benefit from AI: PwC (56% of CEOs report no significant financial benefit) and Deloitte (only 10–15% report significant ROI). The Dun & Bradstreet counterevidence shows returns are uneven, not that limited returns are rare, so the contradiction condition is not met. The claim holds under the fair plain reading, though no audited net ROI measure exists.
